content: Nutritional support for critically ill children has not been extensively studied, and it remains a contentious issue in pediatric intensive care. Currently, there are no definitive guidelines regarding the optimal type or timing of nutrition for critically ill infants and children. This review is an update of a previous publication from 2009. The primary aim of this review was to evaluate the effects of enteral and parenteral nutrition administered during the first week of critical illness on clinically significant outcomes in pediatric patients. Two main hypotheses were proposed: first, that the mortality rate of critically ill children receiving enteral or parenteral nutrition differs from those who receive no nutrition; and second, that the mortality rate of children receiving enteral nutrition differs from those receiving parenteral nutrition. Subgroup analyses were planned to determine whether the effects of these nutritional interventions varied based on age (infants under one year versus children aged one year or older) or patient type (medical patients admitted for illness without prior surgical intervention versus surgical patients admitted for postoperative or trauma care). Additional secondary hypotheses were also proposed, including whether mortality rates differ between children receiving enteral nutrition alone versus a combination of enteral and parenteral nutrition, and whether mortality rates differ between children receiving combined enteral and parenteral nutrition versus no nutrition at all. For this updated review, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EMBASE, ISI Web of Science, and others, covering studies published up to February 2016. Trial registries, reference lists, conference proceedings, and expert consultations were also utilized. No restrictions were placed on language or publication status. Studies were included if they were randomized controlled trials involving pediatric patients aged one day to 18 years, admitted to a pediatric intensive care unit (PICU), and receiving nutrition within the first seven days of admission. Eligible studies needed to report at least one predefined outcome, such as 30-day or PICU mortality, PICU or hospital length of stay, ventilator days, or complications like nosocomial infections. Studies focusing solely on nutritional outcomes, quality of life, or economic factors were excluded. Additionally, this review did not address other aspects of pediatric nutrition, such as immunonutrition or alternative methods of delivering enteral nutrition. Two authors independently screened the search results, applied inclusion criteria, and assessed the risk of bias. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion. Data extraction was performed by one author and verified by another for accuracy. The quality of evidence was evaluated based on study limitations, consistency of findings, precision, relevance, and potential publication bias. Only one relevant randomized controlled trial was identified. This study involved 77 critically ill children with burns covering more than 25% of their total body surface area. Participants were randomized to receive enteral nutrition either within 24 hours or after at least 48 hours. The trial found no statistically significant differences between the groups in terms of mortality, sepsis, ventilator days, length of stay, unexpected adverse events, resting energy expenditure, nitrogen balance, or albumin levels. The trial was assessed as having an unclear risk of bias, and the quality of evidence was deemed very low due to the small sample size and the presence of only one trial. A protocol for a relevant randomized controlled trial investigating the effects of withholding early parenteral nutrition while completing enteral nutrition in critically ill pediatric patients was identified in the most recent search update, but no results have been published to date. In conclusion, only one randomized trial addressed the review question, and the evidence is of very low quality. There is an urgent need for further research to establish evidence-based guidelines on the timing and types of nutrition for critically ill infants and children.
